newsitem.title: CHILE: BHP may be interested in Chilean mega-port.
newsitem.headline: BHP may be interested in Chilean mega-port.

text.p: Australia's Broken Hill Pty, which owns the Escondida copper mine, may be interested in building or operating a giant new port planned for the town of Mejillones, chairman Jerry Ellis said.

Pre-feasibility studies have begun for the port, which government planners say could eventually ship the bulk of Chile's copper output and become an outlet for "bioceanic corridors" to be built across the continent to Argentina and Brazil.
Ellis said BHP's potential interest in the port would be as a shipment point for copper from Escondida, due to become the world's first million-tonne-a-year copper mine in the next decade.

"The general area of infrastructure concessions is not of interest to BHP. To the extent that they serve our main interest, mining, we may develop into other areas. But at this time, we're concentrating on (mining)," Ellis told a news conference in Santiago.
Asked if BHP was interested in bidding for a concession to build the port, alone or with others, he said it was too early to say for sure.

"We could be interested in participating in its construction or its operation, but far more important is that there be an efficient port in the region," said Ellis, head of the Australia-Chile Business and Investment Council.

The capacity of the aging Antofagasta port, about 60 km south of Mejillones, was being stretched to the limit by the booming copper industry, a trend which will eventually be felt in costs, said Ellis.
"The Antofagasta port is quite old and operating at quite a high level of its capacity," said Ellis, whose company owns 57.5 percent of Escondida, about 170 km inland from Antofagasta.

"With the increasing volume of copper cathodes being produced in the region, and probably the import of acid in greater volumes and maybe even further export of concentrates, there is a sensible question about whether a new port should be built. And Mejillones seems to be the best location for that," he said.

BHP transport and engineering experts have been working on the prefeasibility study, together with other companies in the area "because there is a whole number of people interested in this," said Ellis.

Escondida ships its cathodes out of Antofagasta, as do Codelco and other copper producers across northern Chile. But with concentrates, which form about 80 percent of its production, Escondida has already taken matters into its own hands and built a pier at Puerto de Coloso, a few km south of Antofagasta.
The Mejillones port promises to be one the biggest public works projects in Chile's history, Chilean government planners say.

They envision the port as gradually replacing the urban, congested Antofagasta in much the same way as the modern San Antonio port near Santiago has been gradually taking over from Valparaiso, surpassing it in 1995 to become Chile's main port in terms of cargo volume.
Pre-feasibility studies for Mejillones should be finished in a year or so and there are no cost estimates yet, said Ellis.
Government officials say the new port will be built to handle a new generation of huge ocean-going freighters too large for all but a handful of ports worldwide.

They envision the port, likely to be built through private concessions granted by the government, eventually becoming an outlet for new highways to span the South American continent and bring Brazilian and Argentine grains to the Pacific.
Known as bioceanic corridors, the highways could also have the northern cities of Iquique and Arica as outlets while Peru has been pushing for its port of Ilo as another option.

Australian pension fund administrator AMP, which already has a joint mining exploration venture with Codelco, may also be interested in Mejillones "if it looks to be a viable and profitable opportunity," said AMP official Andrew Threadgold.
